articles.body:
The Queensland leader of a group opposing the eradication of fire ants in Australia has been convicted of obstructing government officers, after a magistrate threw out his argument that the commonwealth-funded program is illegal.

Trevor Hold was fined $1,500 but a conviction was not recorded. Hold has described himself as an “ultrapreneur”, a mental health counsellor, an organic cattle farmer and the chief executive officer of the anti-program group the Australian Advocacy Group – and as self-employed.

He was convicted last month of two counts of obstruction for attempting to prevent fire ant treatment at his property, in what is believed to be a Queensland first.

His organisation and others held a series of well attended meetings last year across south-east Queensland to advise residents on what the group called their legal rights to refuse or prevent access to their properties to the program.

Under Queensland’s Biosecurity Act, landholders must permit program officers to access their property to treat fire ants, which are a declared priority pest.

But the organisations advised landholders to use a provision in the act allowing them to obstruct an officer if they had a “reasonable excuse” to refuse access, a provision in the Biosecurity Act.

On 16 April at about 9.20am, Hold prevented officers from entering his property in Adare in the Lockyer Valley, west of Brisbane. The property was in the treatment zone and due for its annual treatment.

The eradication program had informed Hold in advance that it would treat his property that day. A small group of supporters gathered to film and yell at them while they did so, according to court documents.

The scene was later described as “an increasingly rowdy and crowded and dynamic situation” in the Ipswich magistrates court, which heard Hold’s charges last month.

He was arrested by Queensland police after about 40 minutes for obstructing them by not allowing a gate to be opened. He was then un-arrested. Despite being warned again, he was again arrested after another interaction with program officers.

Hold made three arguments to the magistrate, Leanne Scoines, in his defence.

He argued that he was intimidated by the police and the program officers and “withdrew his consent for their attendance”, describing himself as “frazzled”.

“It was put to Mr Hold that he was not frazzled, and that he had said on three occasions, as heard in the body-worn camera footage, that ‘this is the Trevor Hold show’,” Scoines said.

Through his lawyer, solicitor Beatrice Ludwig, Hold argued that the police had failed to take into account his “reasonable excuse” and were therefore acting outside their powers.

Hold based part of his argument on emails he sent to the Department of Primary Industries in December 2024 and January 2025, notices the magistrate described as “unilateral”, “quasi-legal documents … seeking tacit approval by non-response”. The magistrate found they were of no legal effect.

Finally, he challenged the validity of the program, arguing that the prosecution had not proven it was properly authorised under the Biosecurity Act, Scoines said.

All three arguments were dismissed and the magistrate found that the officers were entitled to proceed on the basis that the DPI officers were exercising powers conferred on them by the Biosecurity Act.

“I am not satisfied that Mr Hold was a credible or liable witness on the critical issues in dispute,” she said.

A police prosecutor told the court “In my respectful submission it was clear he was actually enjoying this incident”.

Hold has appealed against the judgment to the district court.

On his website, Hold advertises fundraising efforts for his defence, and also a mooted class action lawsuit against the program.

Hold would not comment on the case.

Southern Cross University professor David Heilpern compared some of the arguments used by Hold to sovereign citizen cases he used to judge as a magistrate in the NSW Northern Rivers region, particularly his claim that he hadn’t consented to fire ant treatment.

“That is a tried and tested argument in terms of many of those who are on the fringe of or deep into the sovereign citizen movement; that you have a right to remove consent from the operations of various laws,” Heilpern said.

“Whether you consent or don’t consent is completely immaterial under the biosecurity legislation.”

articles.title: L’Europa è bersagliata da minacce ai voli di linea
articles.summary: Vari paesi del continente hanno mobilitato l’aviazione militare per scortare gli aerei minacciati da allarmi bomba
articles.preview: Giovedì 5 novembre il trasporto aereo europeo ha vissuto una crisi inedita per come si è svolta e, soprattutto, per la portata. Una ventina di voli di linea sono stati bersaglio di allarmi bomba, costringendo vari paesi a far decollare degli aerei militari per scortarli e dirottarli verso aeroporti diversi dalla loro destinazione iniziale.
articles.body:
Giovedì 5 novembre il trasporto aereo europeo ha vissuto una crisi inedita per come si è svolta e, soprattutto, per la portata. Una ventina di voli di linea sono stati bersaglio di allarmi bomba, costringendo vari paesi a far decollare degli aerei militari per scortarli e dirottarli verso aeroporti diversi dalla loro destinazione iniziale.

In Francia, un Rafale è decollato d’urgenza dalla base aerea 113 di Saint-Dizier-Robinson (Haute-Marne), alle 8.45, per intercettare un Airbus A320 della compagnia irlandese Aer Lingus, che collegava Dublino a Roma, dopo un allarme trasmesso dalle autorità italiane. Intercettato a sud di Parigi, l’aereo è stato scortato fino alla base aerea 105 di Évreux-Fauville (Eure), da dove era decollato anche un Mirage 2000-5 per andare incontro al velivolo.

Scene simili ci sono state in vari altri paesi europei. “A causa di minacce bomba contro aerei civili, tutti i voli interessati nello spazio aereo austriaco sono stati scortati da Eurofighter”, ha dichiarato su X un generale delle forze armate austriache. Un volo Wizz Air che avrebbe dovuto collegare Milano-Malpensa a Varsavia è così atterrato a Vienna. In Bulgaria, alcuni caccia MiG-29 dell’aeronautica militare sono decollati per intercettare e scortare tre aerei Ryanair.

Il ministro dell’interno ceco Lubomír Metnar ha annunciato che quattro aerei atterrati all’aeroporto Václav Havel di Praga sono stati oggetto di un allarme bomba. Due voli provenivano dal Regno Unito, uno dall’Irlanda e uno dalla Grecia: due voli EasyJet, uno Ryanair e uno SkyExpress. Ha aggiunto che era stato preso di mira anche l’aeroporto. La polizia ha ritenuto le minacce poco credibili e, di fatto, non ha trovato nulla dopo aver perquisito gli aerei. A Varsavia, una pista dell’aeroporto principale, Fryderyk Chopin, ha dovuto essere chiusa per consentire i controlli a bordo di un aereo che collegava la capitale polacca a Parigi.

Email di rivendicazione

All’inizio della settimana c’erano stati altri falsi allarmi, ma in numero minore. “Qualsiasi minaccia nei confronti dei civili è inaccettabile”, ha protestato Apostolos Tzitzikostas, commissario europeo ai trasporti. Secondo Tzitzikostas, “è troppo presto per trarre conclusioni su un possibile collegamento tra gli incidenti segnalati. Le indagini nazionali proseguono”. La maggior parte degli allarmi è arrivata nelle prime ore del mattino del 5 novembre, concentrata in un arco di tempo relativamente breve, il che fa supporre un’operazione coordinata.

Le autorità italiane hanno rivelato che giovedì mattina era stata inviata un’email di rivendicazione alla società Aeroporti di Roma da un gruppo che si presentava come i “Combattenti dello stato maschile”, un nome simile a quello dell’organizzazione Stato maschile, un’entità russa fondata nel 2016, messa al bando nel 2021 da un tribunale di Nižnij Novgorod (Russia) e appartenente alla cosiddetta maschiosfera. L’email è stata ricevuta anche dall’aeroporto di Sofia.

Dall’inizio del decennio, l’evoluzione di questa corrente radicale e violenta, vicina all’estrema destra, si è manifestata con un aumento delle azioni terroristiche che hanno colpito soprattutto il Nordamerica e l’Europa. Tuttavia, questa ondata di allarmi bomba sugli aerei si inserisce in un contesto caratterizzato da un’intensificazione delle cosiddette minacce “ibride” contro l’Europa, come dimostrano gli attacchi informatici che di recente hanno preso di mira i supermercati in Francia, il 12 ottobre, e in Italia e in altri paesi europei nella notte tra il 1 e il 2 novembre.

In Francia, l’intervento dei due caccia è avvenuto all’interno della cosiddetta missione permanente di sicurezza aerea affidata all’aeronautica militare e spaziale. Quest’ultima garantisce, 24 ore su 24, sette giorni su sette, una capacità operativa permanente per la sicurezza aerea, sotto l’autorità del primo ministro.

Mobilita quotidianamente 450 aviatori e si basa sul servizio ininterrotto di quattro squadriglie di caccia e tre squadriglie di elicotteri. Secondo la relazione sulla difesa del disegno di legge di bilancio 2027, presentata – e respinta – il 1 ottobre all’Assemblea nazionale, “finora, tra gennaio e la fine di settembre 2026, ci sono stati 712 decolli in allerta, contro i 500 dello stesso periodo del 2025”.

Il procuratore della repubblica di Évreux Rémi Coutin ha annunciato l’apertura di un’indagine nei confronti del pilota irlandese dell’aereo dell’Aer Lingus perché avrebbe “rifiutato”, in un primo momento, di atterrare sulla base militare di Évreux, come chiesto dalle autorità, “preferendo un aeroporto civile”. Il pilota “sarà ascoltato liberamente e in seguito deciderò su un eventuale fermo”, ha dichiarato il magistrato all’Agence France-Presse (Afp), evocando una possibile “violazione del codice dei trasporti”. Giovedì sera, le 157 persone a bordo dell’aereo dirottato verso Évreux sono salite su pullman dirette a Roissy, per proseguire da lì il viaggio verso Roma, riferisce l’Afp. ◆

articles.title: What a Trump-Xi-Putin summit could mean – and what it wouldn’t
articles.summary: A Trump-Xi-Putin meeting at APEC would be a coup for Moscow, analysts say, but Beijing appears lukewarm.
articles.preview: A Trump-Xi-Putin meeting at APEC would be a coup for Moscow, analysts say, but Beijing appears lukewarm. On the sidelines of this month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, an unprecedented three-way meeting between United States President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin could take place.
articles.body:
A Trump-Xi-Putin meeting at APEC would be a coup for Moscow, analysts say, but Beijing appears lukewarm.

On the sidelines of this month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, an unprecedented three-way meeting between United States President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin could take place.

“China is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters in Beijing on Wednesday.

“Work is under way to coordinate such a meeting,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday, adding: “We hope that it will be finalised in the coming days.”

Trump has said he is open to three-way talks focused on nuclear weapons. “If President Xi wants to have it, I’d have it,” he told reporters last month.

The three leaders have met separately but have never held formal talks together.

So could the meeting, pencilled in for November 18-19, actually happen, and what would it mean for the rest of the world? Here’s what we know:

What would Russia get out of a three-way meeting with the US and China?

At the very least, a photo opportunity.

“It is a big event,” Alexander Bratersky, a Moscow-based journalist and political analyst, told Al Jazeera.

He pointed to Pyotr Tolstoy, chairman of the Russian parliament’s foreign affairs committee, who he said has described the meeting as a path towards a new Yalta – the 1945 conference where the leaders of the Soviet Union, the US and the United Kingdom shaped the post-war order in Europe.

That allows Moscow to “talk big”, Bratersky said, while putting Ukraine on the sidelines.

Simply being at the table would make Putin “first among equals”, he added, giving him a photo opportunity to show the world that he will be among those deciding the future of Europe’s security architecture after the war in Ukraine.

If the meeting produced results, he said, it would reflect China’s influence on Russia.

“We should take into account that we are dealing with a much weaker US leader after elections,” Bratersky said.

Trump remains in charge of foreign policy, he explained, but will have less leverage if Democrats, who won control of both chambers of Congress in this week’s midterm elections, start sending money to Kyiv.

“A meeting by itself will be a success,” he said. “Putin will be able to sell it at home”.

Whether anything comes of it should become clear within a month or so, Bratersky said, and the meeting could lead to another during the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami in December.

If nothing is produced before Christmas, he added, “it will be just a photo op.”

What does Trump want?

Optics and leverage.

Trump wants “a personal, high-drama encounter” that lets him claim he is “dealing with” the other two great powers on his own terms, Inderjeet Parmar, a professor of international politics at City St George’s, University of London, told Al Jazeera.

A three-way meeting would allow Trump to present himself as “the indispensable deal-maker”, Parmar said, talking up potential deals on Ukraine, trade, energy or arms control.

“After the midterms the domestic political need for a foreign policy ‘win’ is real,” he said.

Any image of Trump sitting with Xi and Putin could be spun as evidence that American power still commands the table, he said, “even if the substance is limited or largely symbolic”.

“The domestic audience, and his eroding MAGA base, matters at least as much as the diplomatic one,” Parmar said.

What does China want?

Not a summit on Ukraine.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said he raised the idea of discussing Ukraine with Xi when they met in Beijing on October 30, and could see the “surprise” on his face, Germany’s DPA news agency reported.

Steinmeier told public broadcaster ARD that Xi said the three presidents would probably meet in Shenzhen, but not to discuss Ukraine.

He said Xi explicitly pointed out that the Russia-Ukraine war is a European conflict in which the “Europeans must sit at the table”.

Beijing is also likely to swat away Trump’s push for nuclear talks.

Last month, China’s Foreign Ministry said it would be “neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage”.

What would a meeting mean for the rest of the world?

Allies could be sidelined.

Parmar said a three-way meeting would mark “a clear break from the post-1945 pattern”, in which Washington coordinated closely with its European and Asian allies before engaging with Moscow or Beijing.

“A free-standing trilateral [meeting] risks treating those allies as secondary players whose interests can be managed after the fact,” he said, adding that those interests could even be traded.

That would be a shift towards “personalised great-power diplomacy”, he said. But the Trump administration still has hopes to drive a wedge between Russia and China, Parmar added.

Fears of a “G3” are “understandable but overstated in institutional terms”, he said, because the three capitals’ interests diverge sharply on Ukraine, Taiwan, technology and the rules of the international economy.

“The real risk is not a formal G3 secretariat, but the normalisation of great-power deals struck with little consultation of those most affected,” he said.

“History offers many examples of such moments. They rarely produce stable order and often leave the excluded feeling the costs,” Parmar said.

articles.title: Ukraine raises Zaporizhia aid strike death toll to at least 50
articles.summary: Ukrainian officials say DNA tests are being used to identify bodies while up to 39 remain trapped under rubble.
articles.preview: Ukrainian officials say DNA tests are being used to identify bodies while up to 39 remain trapped under rubble. The death toll from a Russian attack on an aid distribution centre in Ukraine’s Zaporizhia region has risen to at least 50 people, making it one of the deadliest Russian attacks this year. Ukraine’s emergency service announced on Friday that the toll from Monday’s strike on the village of Komyshuvakha has risen after eight more bodies were recovered from the rubble.
articles.body:
Ukrainian officials say DNA tests are being used to identify bodies while up to 39 remain trapped under rubble.

The death toll from a Russian attack on an aid distribution centre in Ukraine’s Zaporizhia region has risen to at least 50 people, making it one of the deadliest Russian attacks this year.

Ukraine’s emergency service announced on Friday that the toll from Monday’s strike on the village of Komyshuvakha has risen after eight more bodies were recovered from the rubble.

Acting regional governor Mykhailo Semikin later said that the death toll reached 53 people, as rescuers continued their search for missing bodies for the fifth day.

Al Jazeera was not able to independently verify that figure.

Local police on Wednesday said that 59 people were listed as missing, though some might be among the bodies already found.

“As many as 39 people may still remain trapped under the debris,” they said.

As rescuers continue to work, specialists have been taking DNA samples to identify the bodies. Continuing Russian attacks have also remained a constant threat to the rescue operation.

Ukraine said that Russian aircraft bombed a former school near the front lines on Monday, which civilians used for weekly aid handouts.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a second wave of bombs then hit the underground shelter where people had taken cover, causing most of the destruction.

“After the first aerial bomb strike, there was a double-tap strike with nine more bombs, specifically targeting the shelter where people were taking cover,” he said on X.

Four police officers and two rescue workers were also among the dead.

Zelenskyy called it a “vile terrorist strike” and said it signalled Moscow’s refusal to stop the fighting. The UN human rights mission in Ukraine also said the strike was likely a breach of international law.

The attack on Monday came only a day after a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky ended.

Russia and Ukraine both continued to trade drone attacks on Thursday, which injured several people on both sides, including a child.

On Wednesday, in the eastern Donetsk region, Russian attacks killed four civilians and injured five others.

Delegations from both Ukraine and Russia are expected to meet in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11 for US-brokered talks, though previous rounds made little progress.

articles.title: Zambia's civil service overhaul raises questions
articles.summary: Government-backed retirements and institutional realignments are fueling debate in Zambia, with opposition politicians questioning transparency while officials defend the changes as necessary reforms.
articles.preview: Zambia's opposition criticizes government restructuring and layoffs November 6, 2026 Government-backed dismissals and restructuring are fueling debate in Zambia. Opposition politicians are questioning the transparency of the plans; officials say the changes are necessary. Many people living in Zambia seek careers in the civil service because of the stability and security traditionally associated with government employment.
articles.body:
Zambia's opposition criticizes government restructuring and layoffs

November 6, 2026

Government-backed dismissals and restructuring are fueling debate in Zambia. Opposition politicians are questioning the transparency of the plans; officials say the changes are necessary.

Many people living in Zambia seek careers in the civil service because of the stability and security traditionally associated with government employment. But recent retirements, dismissals and restructuring exercises across several public institutions have unsettled that perception and sparked a national debate about the government's use of "national interest" provisions.

Among those affected is former public relations officer Godfrey Chilabi, whose departure from the Zambia Police Service was announced in October. Choosing not to publicly discuss the circumstances surrounding his exit, Chilabi simply told media that he had been retired in the national interest.

"Yes, I have been retired in national interest," Chilabi said. "I can't give any reason, but know I'm in retirement."

Chilabi's departure came amid a series of changes affecting public institutions in Zambia.

Charity Munganga, a Zambia Police Service deputy inspector general, was dismissed, and all staff members at the Zambia Medicines and Medical Supplies Agency were let go as part of a "reset" following a government audit.

Additionally, all directors in senior management at the Zambia Environmental Management Agency (ZEMA) were put on administrative leave to facilitate an institutional realignment exercise.

The affected ZEMA directors will be assessed for their competence, performance and suitability for their positions before a final decision is made on whether they will be reinstated or separated from the institution, according to an October 20 statement by the Green Economy and Environment Ministry cited by the news portal Mwebantu.

Zambia's public servants on edge

The issue moved to the center of public debate in October, when opposition lawmakers questioned the government in parliament over retirements and dismissals taking place across public institutions following Zambia's general election in August.

Governance and political commentator Andrew Nguvu told DW that retirements carried out in the national interest raise important questions about transparency, fairness and the protection of a professional public service.

"If at all, there are legitimate reasons for retiring any particular civil servant, then obviously the government should clearly explain," Nguvu said.

He said public institutions should operate according to established procedures and the law rather than political considerations that could undermine institutional independence.

Zambian law allows service commissions to retire established officers in the national interest under provisions governing public service employment. Previous governments have also used the measure. However, the current exercise has generated significant scrutiny because it is occurring alongside broader restructuring efforts affecting multiple institutions.

Opposition cries hypocrisy

Critics argue that the issue is particularly sensitive because Zambia's ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) previously opposed the use of retirements in the national interest while in opposition.

As a result, opposition lawmakers, led by Stephen Kampyongo, have criticized the measures, which they view as inconsistent with the ruling party's earlier position.

Kampyongo, speaking during Vice President's Question Time in the National Assembly on October 17, asked what assurances the government was giving public servants, who are "working in fear," and what measures were being taken to ensure that government workers retired in the national interest did not become destitute.

Government pushes back

Responding on behalf of the government, Vice President Mutale Nalumango rejected suggestions that the exercise amounted to a political purge and described it as part of a lawful process of institutional realignment.

Nalumango acknowledged the concerns surrounding the changes but defended the government's authority to make personnel adjustments within the public service framework.

"As provided for in section 39 of the Public Service Pensions Act, there are situations that arise and people fall by the way side," Nalumango told the parliament. "[It is] unfortunate that a life was lost, but maybe it is an issue that public servants/public service workers must brace themselves for."

Nalumango's comments have been cited by critics as evidence that additional changes could occur as the government continues to restructure public institutions.

The debate has been amplified by comments from UPND National Youth Chairperson Gilbert Liswaniso, who said governments naturally sought to work with people aligned with their vision.

"Every political party [that] comes to power has to flush out!" Liswaniso said. "[It] has to work with the people aligned with the vision of that political party!"

Critics say such statements reinforce concerns that political considerations may be influencing decisions within the public service.

The civil rights activist David Chishimba rejects the notion that perceived political affiliation should determine a person's future in government employment.

"The constitution, however, is very clear on this," Chishimba told DW. "It restricts public officers from participating in partisan politics while in office. This safeguards an impartial civil service. However, it does not prohibit private political belief or otherwise."

Chishimba said civil servants served the country rather than any political organization. "Civil servants serve Zambia," he said, "not a party, the president or a campaign."

Workers face uncertainty

Nguvu said the shift was deeply unsettling for public workers caught in the middle of the administrative realignments.

The measures come as the cost of living and household debt burdens increase in Zambia.

Nguvu said abrupt personnel changes could affect morale throughout the public service and leave workers uncertain about their professional future.

"This can weaken morale and help to destroy institutional memory," Nguvu said. "Most of these decisions lack clear explanations."

Nguvu said such concerns had become more acute when explanations for personnel decisions were not communicated clearly.

The reported dismissals have also raised concerns among civil society groups about due process and accountability.

Chishimba, who is also the president of the Zambia Council of Activists (ZACA), called for greater transparency from the authorities.

"ZACA respectfully calls on the government to publish the names and evidence of those facing dismissal, submit every case to due process, and allow the Civil Service Commission to assert its constitutional independence," Chishimba said

articles.title: Russia to UAE, Iran steps up diplomacy amid Trump threats: What we know
articles.summary: Iran launches diplomatic offensive as US mulls resumption of war.
articles.preview: Iran launches diplomatic offensive as US mulls resumption of war. Iran has stepped up diplomatic efforts amid suggestions by United States President Donald Trump that the US could resume full-scale strikes on the Islamic republic. The US news website Axios quoted a US official saying that US Central Command (CENTCOM) was preparing for the resumption of major military operations in Iran, and that it was just waiting on orders from Washington.
articles.body:
Iran launches diplomatic offensive as US mulls resumption of war.

Iran has stepped up diplomatic efforts amid suggestions by United States President Donald Trump that the US could resume full-scale strikes on the Islamic republic.

The US news website Axios quoted a US official saying that US Central Command (CENTCOM) was preparing for the resumption of major military operations in Iran, and that it was just waiting on orders from Washington. On Thursday, Trump told reporters the US may have to “destroy” the rest of Iran, adding that people will “know soon enough” if he acts.

Tehran’s intensified diplomatic push comes after Iran downed two US reconnaissance drones near Qeshm island in the Strait of Hormuz, which the US struck earlier this week. Iran says it will retaliate if the US resumes larger strikes.

What diplomatic efforts is Iran engaging in?

On Thursday, Iran offered the US a new nuclear and peace proposal via Qatari mediators, to be discussed only after Washington meets Tehran’s seven demands, a senior Iranian official told Reuters. The US is examining the proposal, Reuters reported.

Iran has made meeting its seven demands a condition for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and restarting peace talks, including on its nuclear programme. The demands include the lifting of sanctions on Iran, the unfreezing of Iranian assets and the end to the US naval blockade of its ports in and around the Strait of Hormuz, among other things.

It has also stepped up ties with Russia, with its top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, travelling to Moscow for talks on Thursday. During that visit, Rezaei said: “On the issue of diplomacy, we have announced seven conditions to the Americans. As long as they do not execute our seven conditions, we will neither open the Strait of Hormuz nor have negotiations.”

Meanwhile, the US has insisted a deal on Iran’s nuclear capacity must be part of any ceasefire agreement before wider peace talks can restart.

How is Iran deepening ties with Russia?

On Thursday, Rezaei met with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin to deliver a message from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Iranian state media did not elaborate on the contents of the message.

Rezaei called it “an extremely important exchange” according to remarks reported by the Iranian embassy, but also did not give further details.

However, The Financial Times reported that Russia previously agreed to supply Iran with 90 helicopter-mounted launchers for precision-guided missiles, despite needing its own weapons for the Ukraine war. The newspaper cited a Russian defence manufacturer’s production schedule for 2024 and 2025, which it has examined, showing an order for helicopter-mounted launchers being assigned a code used to refer to Iran in Russian defence documents.

Relations between Russia and Iran have deepened since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and during the US-Israeli war on Iran that saw the two countries become the most heavily sanctioned in the world. Iran has provided Shahed drones, which Russia has modified and used heavily against Ukraine.

In return, Russia has also reportedly helped Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles, sold it Verba shoulder-launched anti-air missiles and shared information with Tehran potentially relevant to nuclear weapons.

“It is indicative of Russia’s willingness to continue supplying Iran despite its own wartime demands and with far less concern about Western objections than in the past,” Nicole Grajewski, a non-resident scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told the FT.

In early October, Putin said Russia was prepared to take part in mediation to bring an end to the war.

Images released by the Kremlin showed its foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov and chief of the Russian military intelligence, Igor Kostyukov, attending a meeting with Iran’s security chief alongside Putin.

The meeting also strengthened Iran’s economic ties with Russia.

“During the meeting with Mr Vladimir Putin, discussions were held regarding the construction of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran,” said Rezaei, Iranian state TV reported.

He said the gas pipelines would address Iran’s gas shortages and facilitate the sale of Russian energy to neighbouring countries.

Tehran said Iran’s natural gas refineries had been hit during the most intense phase of US-Israeli strikes on Iran earlier this year, which lasted 40 days.

Separately, Russia’s Foreign Ministry advised citizens against travel to Iran “In light of the remaining risks of a new escalation around Iran”.

How is Iran negotiating with regional leaders?

During the most intense fighting of the war, Iran struck bases in Gulf countries hosting US military assets, as well as civil and energy facilities and infrastructure.

Senior Iranian officials have repeatedly warned that any state helping the US to target the Islamic republic will be a “legitimate target” should US attacks resume.

On Thursday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held phone calls with several Gulf leaders, including the foreign minister of the UAE, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

They discussed regional developments as well as diplomatic efforts for stability in the region, according to Araghchi’s Telegram channel.

Araghchi spoke with Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud about efforts to improve security and stability in the region, according to the Saudi foreign ministry.

Araghchi also discussed de-escalation efforts with the foreign ministers of Kuwait and Turkiye.

In a separate call, Araghchi talked with Qatar’s Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani about coordinating to reduce tensions, the Qatari foreign ministry said.

Sheikh Mohammed stressed support for efforts to secure freedom of maritime navigation.

In a statement, Oman’s foreign ministry said the safety of passage through the Strait of Hormuz was a main topic of discussions, in a call between Araghchi and Oman’s foreign minister.

Iran continues to tightly control shipping lanes through the strait, where several ships have been damaged in recent days. It has granted exemptions to shipping restrictions to Iraq and Qatar, in the Gulf region, as well as to India and China.

What is Trump saying?

Despite his Republican Party suffering a drubbing in this week’s US midterm elections – largely because of public anger over the war on Iran and the resulting rise in energy prices – US President Donald Trump has refused to rule out further strikes on Iran.

On Thursday, Trump told reporters at the Oval Office that he may have to “destroy the rest” of Iran.

Former Iranian diplomat Hadi Afghahi told Al Jazeera that Tehran can ease the path to a settlement if the US also shows flexibility. He argued that Trump “really does not want to go to war, because war again will cost him more”. However, the US president’s next move is unpredictable, observers say.

Afghahi cautioned that Trump “is still surrounded by a group of hawks”, including the energy and treasury secretaries.

Trump has shown willingness to engage in diplomacy, however. Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani discussed diplomatic efforts to ease regional tensions in a phone call with Trump on Friday, according to the Qatari Emiri Diwan.

The leaders reviewed international diplomatic efforts, including the Doha-led mediation efforts to support negotiations in recent weeks, in a bid to reach “a comprehensive agreement that puts an end to the crisis”, the Diwan said in a statement.

How has Iran responded to Trump’s rhetoric?

Tehran warned it will retaliate on a wider scale than it has done so far if the US resumes the war. It has also said talks will become unfeasible.

Iranian officials said Iran has the capacity to strike further than the Gulf using weapons manufactured in Iran.

On Thursday, a spokesman for the Supreme Advisor to the Commander of the Aerospace Force of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said: “In the event of a new aggression, any country or force that helps America attack Iran can be a legitimate target of the Islamic Republic.”

Iran’s state media outlet Tasnim News reported: “Our missile bases have a suitable range to target the Zionist regime and American bases,” adding “Iran’s response to the possible new aggression of the enemies will not be geographically limited.”

Iran has also previously warned that cables, data centres and artificial intelligence (AI) facilities across the Gulf region could be attacked if war with the US erupts again.

What strikes have there been in recent days?

In the run-up to the midterm elections, the US said it had conducted “defensive strikes” on Iran’s Qeshm island and Bandar Lengeh in the Strait of Hormuz.

Meanwhile, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps navy says at least seven tankers have caught fire after sailing into mines while attempting to transit through the Strait of Hormuz using “unauthorised routes” near Oman this week.

Two oil tankers caught fire and were brought to a stop after hitting mines on Friday, the IRGC said. They had been trying to cross the waterway “with the support of the aggressor and terrorist American military”, the IRGC added.

Control over the Strait of Hormuz has been a main stumbling block in negotiations to end the Iran war since it began in February.

Tehran has sought to limit traffic through the strategic waterway, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil supplies.

The US has also imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and escorted tankers through the strait.

Maritime organisations have not confirmed the latest incidents.

articles.title: Fake Iranian accounts ‘campaigned for Netanyahu’ ahead of Israeli election
articles.summary: Fake Iranian accounts ‘campaigned for Netanyahu’ ahead of Israeli election Submitted by MEE staff on Fri, 11/06/2026 - 11:17 Network of 1,653 X profiles reportedly pushed Israelis to back Likud in coordinated Hebrew posts, then went back to promoting the shah’s son Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks following exit polls in Jerusalem on 28 October (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters) Off A network of 1,653 X accounts posing as Iranian users amplified Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s election campaign ahead of last week’s vote, Haaretz reported on Friday. The accounts posted messages in Hebrew urging Israelis to vote for Netanyahu “on behalf of the Iranian people”. The accounts, which claimed to belong to Iranians living in Iran or abroad, appeared to coordinate their activity. Their operators remain unidentified. Activity intensified on election day, when multiple accounts published identical messages and responded to posts in coordinated bursts. Two accounts, for example, shared 109 identical posts, compared with just four expected through organic activity, according to Haaretz’s analysis. They also responded simultaneously, or within five minutes of each other, to 232 posts by 53 different accounts. On election morning, two accounts posted the same Hebrew message about an hour apart: “We call on you to support Benjamin Netanyahu to finish the job”, accompanied by the hashtag #IsraeliElections2026. “Tomorrow, vote only for the Likud party,” one account wrote in response to a Netanyahu post at 10pm on the eve of the election. “Vote for Benjamin Netanyahu,” another posted twice within two minutes after midnight. “Dear people of Israel, if you want to be protected from the Islamic Republic and the Axis of Resistance, vote,” read another message, published in Hebrew and English at around 2am. Haaretz reported that the findings were based on research by Expose, a social media monitoring company that specialises in tracking digital influence operations and disinformation. The investigation follows an earlier Haaretz report that found accounts previously linked to an influence campaign targeting Iran’s government had begun engaging with Israel’s election campaign and amplifying Netanyahu’s videos. Israel’s Netanyahu accused of attempting coup after election defeat d a petition with the Central Elections Committee over the accounts identified in the investigation. Expose found that around 1,600 of the accounts had been identified last year as part of an influence operation promoting Reza Pahlavi, the son of Iran’s last shah, who was overthrown in 1979, as an alternative to the Iranian government. As Israel’s election campaign gathered pace in July, 185 of these accounts began interacting with Netanyahu’s social media profiles, including by sharing posts attacking his political opponents. According to Haaretz, the network returned to its usual focus on Pahlavi after the election concluded last week. Some of the findings were submitted to the Central Elections Committee in October as expert evidence in a petition brought by the Brandeis Institute and FakeReporter against Netanyahu, Likud and the Prime Minister’s Office. The committee’s chairman, Judge Noam Solberg, rejected the petition on the eve of the election. Solberg ruled that the network’s activity was subject to election advertising transparency requirements and appeared, on the face of it, to violate the law. However, he said the committee could not reach a definitive ruling because the identities of those operating the accounts were unknown. He ordered the evidence to be referred to the police. In response to the investigation published in October, the Prime Minister’s Office and Likud denied any connection to the accounts. articles.title: 'No choice but to bear it': Delhi's unrelenting air pollution crisis
articles.summary: Despite years of government interventions, emergency restrictions and public outrage, Delhi continues to battle dangerously polluted air every winter. Why isn't there a lasting solution to a predictable crisis?

articles.body:
November 6, 2026

Despite years of government interventions, emergency restrictions and public outrage, Delhi continues to battle dangerously polluted air every winter. Why isn't there a lasting solution to a predictable crisis?

On a slightly chilly and distinctly smoggy morning in New Delhi, Khushboo Arora was looking for another air purifier for her mother, who has underlying health complications, before the city's air quality deteriorated further.

"Already, I am starting to get a recurring headache," she said. "These days when I wake up, I don't feel fresh. As the day progresses, I feel a heaviness in my head, itching in my eye and a constantly parched throat."

Not long ago, the unpacking of woolens announced the advent of winter in Delhi. Now, it's the light hum of an air purifier in the corner.

Arora said she has already stopped doing yoga in the park and taking her morning walks. She has also filled her house with air-purifying plants and started spraying water mist inside the house to bring down the level of pollution.

"My parents look at me like I have gone mad. But I feel people are not realizing the gravity of the situation," she said.

A recurring crisis

Winters in Delhi increasingly follow a familiar pattern: Air quality deteriorates, residents struggle to breathe, emergency restrictions kick in and governments exchange blame. Then the season changes, only for the cycle to repeat the following year.

On Thursday, Delhi's air fell into the "Very unhealthy" category, according to Swiss air quality monitor IQAir, with an average PM2.5 concentration of 157.9 micrograms per cubic meter of air. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends an annual safe limit of no more than 5 micrograms.

Studies have shown that exposure to PM2.5 — air particles with a diameter smaller than 2.5 micrometers that can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream — is associated with an increased incidence of head and neck cancer (HNC), like oral, nasal and throat cancers.

But despite years of attempted interventions, India's capital continues to struggle with the same pollution crisis.

What is causing the air pollution?

Delhi is not dealing with an unknown problem. There is considerable scientific understanding of its causes.

A 2026 assessment by an expert panel reviewed by the Delhi government identified the major winter contributors of PM2.5 as vehicular emissions, industrial activity, road and construction dust, biomass and waste burning, and pollution from neighboring regions.

Sunil Dahiya, founder of the environmental group EnviroCatalysts, said Delhi is part of a larger airshed. On most winter days, more pollution comes into Delhi than is generated inside it, according to the environmentalist.

"Analysis of the government's Decision Support System (DSS) data for winter 2025 found that around 65% of Delhi's PM2.5 came from outside the city and about 35% from sources within it," he told DW, adding that neighboring Noida and Gurugram, which comprise the National Capital Region (NCR), are some of the biggest contributors.

Coordinating action across the NCR, which spans Delhi and parts of three neighboring states, remains a major obstacle.

"This is a shared problem, and no single city can solve it alone," Dahiya said.

Why aren't anti-pollution policies working?

To understand why existing policies have not delivered sustained improvements, Dahiya highlighted the gap between scientific recommendations and state action.

"Scientists have said for over a decade that we need airshed-wide, year-round, source-specific action. What we mostly get is seasonal and reactive," he said.

According to the environmentalist, emergency restrictions kick in only after pollution has reached dangerous levels. Short-term measures such as water sprinklers and smog towers provide little relief, while bigger structural changes are slow to materialize. These include stricter enforcement of industrial emissions, cleaner fuels, expanded public transport, vehicle electrification and viable alternatives to crop burning for farmers.

"The science is not the bottleneck. Implementation, regional coordination and political will are," said Dahiya. "Until targets are tied to emission reductions at each source, and someone is held accountable for meeting them, we will keep having the same conversation every November."

Bhavreen Kandhari, co-founder of Warrior Moms, agrees that official responses focus on reacting rather than preventing.

"They allow pollution to occur and then try to clean it up — producing nice photo opportunities of water sprinklers and smog guns, or talking about cloud seeding," Kandhari told DW. "Creating pollution only to clean it up later is a waste of public funds, time, and health."

Kandhari also added that incinerating waste instead of proper waste management has only exacerbated the situation.

The politics of pollution

Another obstacle to a lasting solution has been the political blame game that starts as soon as the air quality worsens.

On Thursday, Delhi Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa said stubble-burning in the neighboring state of Punjab is contributing to the capital's rising pollution, according to public broadcaster All India Radio. He insisted that in Delhi, construction, vehicle and industrial sources were controlled.

Dahiya agreed that seasonal crop-burning fires in neighboring states of Punjab and Haryana "is an episodic but sharp contributor" which "can tip 'very poor' air into 'severe'" for a few weeks. But it is not the lone contributor.

"Among sources within Delhi, vehicles alone contribute roughly 51-53% of local PM2.5. A large share of winter PM2.5 is also secondary particulate formed from gases like sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and ammonia," Dahiya said. "That points straight back to combustion in power plants, industry and transport."

"If stubble burning ended tomorrow, Delhi would still breathe unhealthy air for most of the year," he added.

DW reached out to several Delhi government officials for a response, but received no reply.

What needs to change?

Delhi is also home to millions of people who cannot afford air purifiers and have no escape from the toxic air.

Among them is Deepika, who works as domestic help in an affluent South Delhi neighborhood. She has been coughing for a week.

It is the same every year, she said.

"I have no choice but to bear it for the next few months."

The people DW spoke to point to a common set of priorities: Addressing Delhi's pollution crisis requires year-round pollution control rather than seasonal restrictions, better coordination between governments and stronger enforcement of existing regulations and measurable targets. They say the city needs a sustained clean-air strategy more than another winter emergency plan.

Namrata Yadav is a Delhi resident and the mother of an eight-year-old boy. They both joined protests against air pollution in November. A year later, the problems persist.

"It is exhausting to repeat the same things year after year, only to be dismissed as paranoid or alarmist for demanding something as basic as clean air," she said.

Calling for lasting solutions driven by science, policy and accountability, Yadav said: "We have spent years learning how to live with pollution. It is time we demanded that those responsible learn how to end it."

articles.title: ‘Quiet crisis’: Government expert panel convenes to tackle population decline
articles.summary: The panel discussed how to reverse the declining birthrate trend, how to build sustainable local communities and how to cope with labor shortages.
articles.preview: Japan convened its first panel of experts Friday to help draft a plan to reverse the country’s declining birthrate and restructure its socioeconomic systems to cope with a shrinking population. “Population decline is a national crisis that is unfolding quietly,” Minoru Kiuchi, minister for economic and fiscal policy, said at the meeting.
articles.body:
Japan convened its first panel of experts Friday to help draft a plan to reverse the country’s declining birthrate and restructure its socioeconomic systems to cope with a shrinking population.

“Population decline is a national crisis that is unfolding quietly,” Minoru Kiuchi, minister for economic and fiscal policy, said at the meeting.

The panel traded ideas on how to reverse the declining birthrate trend, how to build sustainable local communities, and how Japan should aim to become a society where those who wish to marry or have children “don’t have to make excessive sacrifices,” Kiuchi said.

AI’s potential to address labor shortages was also discussed among panel members, he said.

Japan’s population is aging rapidly. Despite a slight increase of births in the first half of this year, the number was far outpaced by the number of deaths, at 320,458 and 766,746, respectively. Last year, the country’s fertility rate was 1.14, the lowest on record.

According to projections released by the National Institute of Population and Social Security Research (IPSS) in 2023, the country’s population could fall below 100 million by 2056 and decline to 87 million by 2070 under its medium-fertility scenario. A lower-fertility scenario puts the population at about 80 million by 2070.

When asked about foreign workers at a briefing following the meeting, Akira Kurosawa, secretary of the cabinet’s headquarters for population strategy, said that panel discussions ranged from concerns about over-reliance, efforts to improve working conditions, and worries about labor shortages if foreign worker numbers are reduced.

The panel consists of 14 members, primarily academics specializing in sociology and economics, as well as business executives and a department head from the IPSS. Former internal affairs and communications minister, Hiroya Masuda, will serve as the chairman.

The government will draw on the expert panel’s views on three fertility-rate scenarios and assumptions about the number of foreign nationals to conduct simulations of Japan’s future population. The results, expected to be incorporated into the comprehensive population strategy by December, will also inform the government’s basic policy on accepting foreign nationals, which is due to be finalized by March.

The government held its first meeting of senior vice ministers responsible for developing the strategy on Oct. 28, establishing a framework for coordinating policies across ministries.

Kiuchi said the government would continue working with the experts and across ministries and agencies to develop the strategy.

articles.title: Trump denounces 'crooked' US midterms after Republican debacle
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump on Thursday denounced "crooked" elections after the Democrats' victory in this week's midterms.
articles.preview: USA US President Donald Trump lashed out at "crooked" elections Thursday as the Democrats' midterm steamroller powered ahead, with another potential Senate upset in Mississippi threatening to deepen Republicans' historic defeat. "Our elections are so crooked, you have no idea," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, as he denounced the "disgraceful" victory of a democratic socialist in the Los Angeles mayoral race.
articles.body:
USA

US President Donald Trump lashed out at "crooked" elections Thursday as the Democrats' midterm steamroller powered ahead, with another potential Senate upset in Mississippi threatening to deepen Republicans' historic defeat.

"Our elections are so crooked, you have no idea," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, as he denounced the "disgraceful" victory of a democratic socialist in the Los Angeles mayoral race.

His outburst came just two days after Americans handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress in a sweeping rejection of Trump's presidency and the Republican Party he has remade in his image.

Trump has repeatedly lashed out against so-called rigged elections in the past, most notably after his 2020 presidential loss.

Although Trump initially accepted the midterm results, he has since demanded that votes cast for two minor candidates in Alaska's still-undecided Senate race be handed to the trailing Republican incumbent.

Trump has refused to take any responsibility for his party's debacle in the midterms. Meanwhile, US Vice President JD Vance has tried to distance himself from Trump and has blamed the Iran war for the losses.

The president's renewed attacks on the electoral process contrast with a political landscape transformed by Tuesday's Democratic landslide.

Democrats are already set to hold at least 54 Senate seats to the Republicans' 44. Their House majority surged past 250 seats on Thursday, the party's biggest in almost two decades.

After Trump warned that he would use his veto power to block Democratic legislation, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer issued a warning of his own.

"If Donald Trump does spend the next year vetoing common sense legislation to lower costs and end corruption, this election — this absolute Republican catastrophe on election night 2026 — will look like a good day compared to what will come down on Republicans in the 2028 election," Schumer said.

Mississippi, Alaska nail-biters

The biggest remaining midterms nail-biter was in Mississippi, one of the most solidly Republican states in the nation, where against all expectations a 43-year-old Black candidate, Scott Colom, appeared to be on the cusp of winning a US Senate seat.

By afternoon, Colom's lead ahead of incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith was inching up at 1,724 votes and only a handful of ballots left to count. The final result could take days to come.

Colom would be the first Democrat to win a Senate seat from the southern state since 1982 — and the first African American to do so since 1874.

In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola was also just ahead of the pack with 48.17 % of the vote, followed by Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan with 47.88 %.

Trump's Truth Social outburst referred to a fringe candidate also named Dan Sullivan, whom Republicans accuse of being a "decoy" aimed at siphoning votes from their candidate, and another minor contender Gerald Heikes, who is registered as a Republican.

Trump posted that all the votes for the "Fake" Sullivan and Heikes "should be immediately given to the REAL Dan Sullivan."

"There is no other fair solution!"

Making history

If Colom wins in Mississippi, he would join a host of other new faces smashing racial and cultural barriers in the midterms.

Keisha Lance Bottoms, the great-great-granddaughter of a slave, became the first Black female governor of Georgia — and in the country.

And Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed beat a Trump ally to become the first Muslim to enter the US Senate.

Tuesday's midterms also featured wins for Democrats in political territory where Trump had previously been so dominant that it was all but written off by the left.

James Talarico broke a 38-year hoodoo by winning a Senate seat in ultra-Republican Texas and Adam Hamilton did even better, becoming the first Democratic senator from Kansas in 94 years.

Republican congressman Warren Davidson, in Ohio, said Trump's months-long war against Iran and global trade wars had lost the election for the party.

Young voters in particular, he said, felt "betrayed."

articles.title: Arab parties back Eisenkot as Israel faces coalition deadlock
articles.summary: Israeli President Isaac Herzog said he will announce on Sunday whom he will task with trying to form a new government, after the opposition's Gadi Eisenkot secured a commanding number of recommendations to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
articles.preview: Israel Israeli President Isaac Herzog said he will announce on Sunday whom he will task with trying to form a new government, after the opposition's Gadi Eisenkot secured a commanding number of recommendations to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Herzog held a second day of consultations with political parties on Thursday after the October 27 election, in which neither Netanyahu -- a polarising right-winger who has led Israel through three years of war -- nor Eisenkot -- a former military chief promising to restore national unity -- secured…
articles.body:
Israel

Israeli President Isaac Herzog said he will announce on Sunday whom he will task with trying to form a new government, after the opposition's Gadi Eisenkot secured a commanding number of recommendations to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Herzog held a second day of consultations with political parties on Thursday after the October 27 election, in which neither Netanyahu -- a polarising right-winger who has led Israel through three years of war -- nor Eisenkot -- a former military chief promising to restore national unity -- secured enough votes for a majority.

Herzog will make his choice, but traditionally the mandate is given to the person recommended by more parliament members. Sixty-seven picked Eisenkot, 46 opted for Netanyahu, while seven abstained.

"The results of the consultations may appear clear, but the authority vested in me by law is to determine who has the ability to form a government, and that is not entirely clear, given the mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves," Herzog said on Thursday.

"I will try to determine this directly and quickly, in personal talks with some of the party leaders."

Eisenkot's Yashar party said on Thursday that "the citizens of Israel have chosen change and expressed a complete lack of confidence in outgoing Prime Minister Netanyahu and his government", and called for the "immediate establishment of a national emergency government that will begin working for all citizens of Israel".

Two Arab-majority lists won an unprecedented 19 seats in the election, making them potential kingmakers if Eisenkot's opposition chooses to work with them, which remains unclear.

Both Arab lists on Thursday said they were backing Eisenkot.

However, another party in Eisenkot's camp, right-wing Israel Beiteinu, has repeatedly indicated it will not sit in a government that relies on support from Arab parties.

Party leader Avigdor Liberman, a former Netanyahu ally turned critic, cited as a reason the refusal by Arab parties to explicitly define Hamas as a "terror group" -- even though they have repeatedly condemned the organisation's attack on Israel on October 7, 2023.

- Ultra-Orthodox exemptions -

Meanwhile, United Torah Judaism, which backed Netanyahu after the previous five elections, in its meeting with Herzog declined to recommend Netanyahu again as premier, although it also did not side with Eisenkot.

The party informed Herzog "that it has decided not to recommend any member of Knesset to form a government", the president's office said in a statement, referring to the 120-member parliament in which United Torah Judaism won seven seats.

Alongside Shas, another ultra-Orthodox party, they have pushed to maintain the exemption from military service for religious students.

Netanyahu has preserved the exemption but stopped short of enshrining it in law, in the face of major resentment from many other Israelis, as reservists serve multiple tours due to the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

"In whatever government is next formed, our immediate item is sorting out the status of Torah students," United Torah Judaism lawmaker Isaac Pindrus said.

Eisenkot, who has tried to appeal to secular Israelis from left to right, has been adamant about ending exemptions for military service.

Some of his opposition allies have criticised the ultra-Orthodox -- who make up about 14 percent of the population but have far higher birthrates than secular Israelis -- as a drain on the state.

Observers say United Torah Judaism's tactic is likely aimed mostly at punishing Netanyahu and showing that their votes cannot be taken for granted, while they would still serve in a government if he were to form one.

- Arab parties play key role -

Once Herzog gives his mandate to a lawmaker, the person will have 28 days to form a government, with a potential 14-day extension. If the lawmaker fails, Herzog will then task someone else.

Netanyahu's bloc, including United Torah Judaism, has 53 seats in the new parliament, compared to 48 for Eisenkot's bloc.

Arab-majority parties scored historic gains on the back of anger over Netanyahu's hard-right government and longstanding complaints about racism from some ministers and discriminatory treatment of Arab Israelis.

Netanyahu has relentlessly attacked the opposition for even the prospect of an alliance with Arab lawmakers.

In a video Wednesday, Netanyahu alleged there were "serious suspicions" that foreign powers put money into the election and questioned the loyalty of Arab citizens.

articles.title: What to know about the presidential wiretapping scandal rocking Indonesia
articles.summary: The scandal involves senior members of President Prabowo Subianto's government, and hint at growing tensions among its elites.
articles.preview: Authorities are investigating possible treason in Indonesia after a bombshell announcement this week that President Prabowo Subianto's phone conversations might have been spied on. Several senior figures of Prabowo's administration have been embroiled in the wiretapping scandal, including his chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - who is not related to the president despite his name.
articles.body:
Authorities are investigating possible treason in Indonesia after a bombshell announcement this week that President Prabowo Subianto's phone conversations might have been spied on.

Several senior figures of Prabowo's administration have been embroiled in the wiretapping scandal, including his chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - who is not related to the president despite his name.

It is unfolding against what many have interpreted as a widening rift between Prabowo and his predecessor, Joko Widodo - otherwise know as Jokowi - who had thrown his support behind Prabowo's 2024 presidential campaign.

"Listyo's position, as we know, is actually very close to Jokowi," Made Supriatma, a visiting fellow at Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, told BBC Indonesian.

"So now it's practically said that they're going their separate ways."

What happened?

Listyo Sigit Prabowo, the president's chief of staff, was arrested on Tuesday along with two senior police officers for allegedly wiretapping President Prabowo.

The three men are suspected of keying phone numbers, including Prabowo's, into the police's official electronic surveillance system - which allows authorities to intercept communications - without following proper procedures, such as obtaining an investigation warrant or case report.

Authorities say the operation was discovered last week after a tip-off from a police officer. But they believe the alleged wiretapping stretches back to 2025, when Listyo was serving as the national police chief.

This could amount to treason, as it involved "sensitive information" that could "endanger the interests and sovereignty of the nation", a spokesperson for the president told reporters on Wednesday.

In Indonesia, treason is punishable by life imprisonment or even the death penalty - though the country has not executed anyone in a decade.

The spokesperson said the motive behind the alleged wiretapping remained unclear.

It was not just President Prabowo who was targeted in the alleged wiretapping operation, either. Other targets included politicians, journalists, NGO representatives and businesspeople, authorities said.

On Thursday evening, police named a fourth suspect: Slamet Uliandi, from the national police criminal investigation unit. But he was not detained due to his ill health after suffering a stroke, according to authorities.

Listyo, who was appointed the president's chief of staff last month, was sacked from his new position shortly after his arrest.

This is not the first wiretapping scandal to have involved Indonesia's leaders. In 2014, several wiretapping devices were discovered at Jokowi's official residence when he was the governor of Jakarta. Former president Megawati Soekarnoputri claimed in 2024 that she had avoided using her personal mobile phone number because she was the target of wiretapping.

Indonesia's police chief Suyudi Ario Seto told reporters on Thursday that the probe into wiretapping was "purely law enforcement and has nothing to do with rivalries or anything else".

But many see it as the latest blow in a disintegrating alliance between President Prabowo and former president Jokowi, who led the country from 2014 to 2024.

Prabowo vs Jokowi

Jokowi had thrown his support behind Prabowo in the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election, as part of an alliance that ultimately propelled Prabowo to become Indonesia's next leader.

Riding to victory with him was Gibran Rakabuming Raka, Jokowi's eldest son, who became Indonesia's vice president.

Two years on, that alliance appears to be fracturing - even if neither party has confirmed the rift.

Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.

In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many of Jokowi's allies into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.

Meanwhile, uncertainty also looms over Gibran, Jokowi's son, who is mired in a growing controversy over the validity of his high school credentials, a pre-requisite to run for vice presidency. He now faces calls to be disqualified from his job, on the grounds that he should not have been eligible as a candidate.

The wiretapping scandal and subsequent arrest of Listyo - who rose to the top of the police force in Jokowi's administration, and is seen as one of the ex-president's longtime allies - is now adding to the tensions between Prabowo and Jokowi.

When asked about the wiretapping incident after the court session on Thursday, Jokowi told reporters that "we should all respect the ongoing legal process".

This latest scandal comes during a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. His flagship free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.

Experts, meanwhile, say all this has distracted from the more pressing challenges that Indonesians are facing on the ground - from economic uncertainties to environmental pollution.

In recent months, protesters have taken to the streets to pressure the government on a range of issues such as toxic wildfire haze, corruption, and cost-of-living woes.

"It's like we're living in a country on autopilot," Nicky Fahrizal, a researcher at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in Indonesia, told BBC Indonesian.

"Because the way the government operates proves that it's not the people's interests that are being pursued, but rather the interests of individual groups."

articles.title: A deadly raid tests a revolutionary town’s faith in Syria's new government
articles.summary: A deadly raid tests a revolutionary town’s faith in Syria's new government Submitted by Natacha Danon on Fri, 11/06/2026 - 10:04 Five people were killed in the town of Rankous after a government raid on alleged Islamic State sympathisers A blue mosque rebuilt by residents stands atop a hill in the small town of Rankous (MEE/Ammar Stifi) Off Driving north from Damascus , I made my way toward the Lebanese border, through barren apple and cherry orchards, up into the Qalamoun mountains. As the town of Rankous came into view, 33-year old Abu Jad, a former member of the Free Syrian Army (FSA) who fought against former ruler Bashar al-Assad, was waiting for me on the main street. He waved at me from the darkened window of his SUV and greeted me with a grim smile. “Welcome to Rankous, the capital of the revolution in Qalamoun,” he said. Early in the morning of 22 October, the town’s habitual calm was shattered when Syrian security forces stormed homes and shops, rounding up 45 people and killing five. According to the Ministry of Interior, the victims had links to the Islamic State (IS), held “extremist ideas,” and had “declared the Syrian state as infidel”. Three of the victims were unarmed at the time, while two opened fire on the security forces, killing two of its members, according to residents. For three consecutive days, hundreds of residents and visitors converged on the town square, where a collective wedding was supposed to be held in less than two weeks’ time. Instead of celebrating life, they were left mourning their sons who had lost their childhood to the war, only to be killed after it finally came to an end. For the people of Rankous, the latest bloodshed has deepened a sense of loss and injustice in a town that gave hundreds of lives to the revolution. Many feel that their community has been left on the margins of the post-Assad order, with little representation in state institutions or support to rebuild. As Syria approaches the second anniversary of Assad’s fall, grievances are quietly growing among many war-scarred communities across the country, with groups like IS poised to exploit them. Descending from his car, Abu Jad extended his left hand to give me a firm handshake, while holding the other tightly against his chest. In 2014, he lost the use of his right arm from a bullet wound. Today, he serves as the media spokesperson for Firas al-Bitar, who founded the FSA-affiliated Sham Liberation Brigade after defecting from the Syrian army in 2012. Residents on Rankous line up in the town square at a funeral for the five men killed by the security forces (Ammar Stifi) A native of Rankous, Bitar rallied hundreds of men from the town to fight against the Syrian regime, leading to its withdrawal in late 2012. In 2014, he and his men fought tooth and nail once again, this time against the Lebanese group Hezbollah, who entered Syria to defend Assad's administration. Overwhelmed by the militia’s firepower, his troops withdrew from the town and were transported to the rebel stronghold of Idlib on the regime’s notorious green buses. But on 8 December 2024, Bitar and his men made a triumphant return to Rankous, cruising in on trucks from northern Syria as Assad’s army crumbled before them. They rode on euphoria for months, until they found themselves sitting at home utterly destitute. A historic rival of the rebel faction that took power in December 2024 - the now officially dissolved Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) - members of FSA factions found themselves sidelined by the new Syrian army being built. According to some media reports, Feras al-Bitar flagged the young men to the authorities due to their connections to Jamal Zainia (nom de guerre Abu Malik al-Talli), a former HTS member still under international sanctions. Abu Jad denied that the raid was linked to a higher-level dispute between him and Zainia. Zainia has also publicly denied involvement in any sort of disagreement. General security raid I got into Abu Jad’s car and we drove to the house of Ahmad al-Khattib, the father of one of the victims, 21-year-old Youssef al-Khattib. He greeted me respectfully at the door and accompanied me to a modest living room, where a dozen men were seated in silence paying him their respects. At 6 o’clock in the morning, the security forces had burst into Youssef’s home, shoving his wife aside as she opened the door. 'He used to dance at weddings and play taekwondo. Plus, I smoke and my son never once reprimanded me - would someone who belongs to IS have been that way?' - Ahmad al-Khattib “Youssef and two friends were seated in the living room drinking matte together after returning from dawn prayers,” his father told me, relaying his wife’s version of the events, who declined to speak to me. “There was an exchange of fire and all three were killed. “We didn’t expect those who carried out the raid to be General Security; we thought they were from Hezbollah perhaps, which explains why my son must have resisted the raid,” Ahmad told me, adding that his home had been occupied by Hezbollah during the war. “He used to dance at weddings and play taekwondo. Plus, I smoke and my son never once reprimanded me - would someone who belongs to IS have been that way? The five boys, my son included, merely had faith in God, nothing more.” Prior to the fall of the Assad regime, Youssef had been providing intelligence to the rebel factions in Idlib. “He was communicating with and supporting Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham from behind the front lines; I didn’t even know until he took up arms the day of the liberation, which gave me great happiness,” his father said, a smile spreading on his face. “However, he only received limited compensation from the state.” Youssef’s younger brother Majd was also an informant for Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham. In 2020, Assad forces raided his home, killing six of his friends and injuring him in his back. “I didn’t feel anything when I was injured because Youssef was by my side; he would carry me around the house,” he told me. “My accident pushed him to also become an informant.” Ahmad al-Khattib stands in the cemetery where his son Youssef is buried (Ammar Stifi) When Assad fell in December 2024, Youssef joined the new Syrian army, but he only lasted a few months because he was deployed to another province and the salary was low. Another knock came at the door, and the men stood to greet Muhammad Suleiman, father of 25-year-old Majd Suleiman, and Muhammad Faraoun, father of 22-year-old Ahmad Faraoun. Majd Suleiman was killed that fateful morning at the small supermarket where he worked in a shootout with the security forces. “He was with the revolution from the age of 10, when he would attend protests with his friends,” his father recalled. Majd spent much of the war hiding at home, as he was wanted by the government for mandatory military service. 'We want justice for the blood of our sons, we want to see those responsible held accountable in court. We joined the revolution to live in freedom and dignity' - Muhammad Faraoun However, Majd, like many other young men of Rankous, was not accepted into the army, citing a lack of available positions. “He wasn’t accepted into the army so, unemployed, he committed himself to [going to] the mosque," he said. His father says he had a good reputation, with no criminal record, and practised taekwondo in his free time. In mid-November, he was supposed to have his wedding, alongside several other young couples. “The wedding was supposed to be in the same square where the funeral is now taking place,” his father said, eyes hollow with grief. “We ask for the spies and informants to be exposed. There are informants now like there were at the time of the regime - nothing has changed, only the accusations,” he added, his voice wavering with anger. The Assad regime maintained a staggering network of informants, who provided real or fabricated intelligence on their coworkers, friends, and even family members. “We want the truth to be revealed and the identities of the informants who are creating social divides to be exposed,” Muhammad echoed. “Our hearts are with the government, but those who wrote security reports [on our sons] and acted on unreliable information are at fault,” chimed in Muhammad Faraoun, father of 22-year old Ahmad Faraoun, a fifth-year student studying information technology. “We want justice for the blood of our sons, we want to see those responsible held accountable in court. We joined the revolution to live in freedom and dignity." Tipping point Ahmad offered to accompany me to the town cemetery, where his son has been laid to rest. We drove to the top of a hill, where hundreds of graves overlook a valley surrounded by the Qalamoun mountains. His grave was unmarked, the brown earth upturned and the tombstone not yet engraved. articles.title: US and Iran edge closer to potential breakthrough in talks to end war, Bloomberg reports
articles.summary: US and Iran edge closer to potential breakthrough in talks to end war, Bloomberg reports The United States and Iran are moving closer to a possible breakthrough in efforts to end the war, with Tehran considering proposals on its nuclear programme that it had previously been unwilling to discuss, Bloomberg reported, citing a diplomat familiar with the talks. The diplomat said Iran was studying proposals on its nuclear activities presented by Qatar, the main mediator. Any concession could help to advance negotiations, which have stalled since the collapse of an interim agreement reached in June. Reuters and The New York Times have also previously reported on Iran’s willingness to compromise on the nuclear issue. US President Donald Trump spoke by phone with Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani about efforts to de-escalate the conflict and secure a comprehensive agreement, the emir’s office said on Friday. Qatari officials have been shuttling between Doha and Tehran to help bridge differences, including over Iran’s nuclear activities and the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

articles.title: Netherlands: Protesters storm Amsterdam data centre construction site
articles.summary: Protesters broke into a data centre construction site intended for Microsoft in Amsterdam, on 6 November, climbing cranes and unfurling banners denouncing artificial intelligence and the company's alleged involvement in the war in Gaza.
articles.preview: Around 100 demonstrators entered the site in the Sloterdijk district, although organisers claimed several hundred had taken part. Activists used ladders to scale the perimeter fence and cut an opening to allow others inside. Some climbed a construction crane, displaying a banner reading "Fuck AI", while others waved Palestinian flags and held signs accusing Microsoft of supporting genocide. Police surrounded the protesters before the mayor ordered the demonstration to end. Riot officers subsequently intervened, with several arrests reported.
