articles.body:
Following this week’s midterms where voters resoundingly voiced their opposition to data center expansion, OpenAI today announced new commitments to communities where it is working on data center projects, including that it won’t use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials.

The ChatGPT maker won’t use NDAs with public officials as part of its new data center community commitments.

Many data center projects have come under scrutiny for relying on NDAs to hide discussions between developers and local officials. However, OpenAI says it is now allowing “only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.” In October, Amazon announced it would no longer use NDAs with government agencies it works with on data center projects.

OpenAI’s additional commitments include paying “the full cost” of electricity it uses and the “infrastructure needed to serve us.” It will make opportunities for local communities by publishing the jobs it expects to create and by reporting on hiring. And every future “compute campus” (its rebranding phrase for data centers) the company owns and operates will have a “local compact” that includes the commitments and will reflect “local priorities,” OpenAI says.

articles.title: Serve Robotics launches new business to become the AWS for robots
articles.summary: Serve Robotics announced alonsgside its third-quarter earnings that it will launch a new business line called Physical AI Services to offer customers its connectivity and data tools.
articles.preview: Serve Robotics, a maker of self-driving sidewalk delivery robots, is expanding beyond its autonomous delivery operations in a bid to become a technology supplier to other companies building robots. The company, which spun out of Uber’s acquisition of Postmates in 2021 and went public in 2024, said Thursday it will launch a new business line called Physical AI Services. Specifically, Serve Robotics will offer customers its connectivity and data tools.
articles.body:
Serve Robotics, a maker of self-driving sidewalk delivery robots, is expanding beyond its autonomous delivery operations in a bid to become a technology supplier to other companies building robots.

The company, which spun out of Uber’s acquisition of Postmates in 2021 and went public in 2024, said Thursday it will launch a new business line called Physical AI Services.

Specifically, Serve Robotics will offer customers its connectivity and data tools. Bedrock Robotics, a startup developing self-driving systems for construction equipment, is a customer, according to Serve. It’s also working with T-Mobile to bring AI computing power closer to robots, Serve announced alongside its third-quarter earnings on Thursday.

“We are solving the problem of robots in human spaces,” Serve Robotics CEO and co-founder Ali Kashani told TechCrunch.

Serve Robotics already makes two kinds of robots, the cute googly-eyed sidewalk delivery robot and one designed for hospitals that it got through its acquisition of Diligent Robotics.

Those businesses are not going away, Kashani emphasized in a recent interview. Instead, he said there is opportunity to sell the technology it developed for its own robots to other companies developing robots for farms, warehouses, and other uncontrolled environments.

“I kind of think of it as the AWS moment where we are taking the technology we’ve built for us, and we’re opening it up for more people to build on,” he said, adding this wouldn’t have been possible without developing its own robot fleet.

The expansion comes as Serve’s sidewalk delivery business expands, but is shifting away from Uber and toward other partners, including DoorDash and Wonder.

Its new Physical AI Services business line will offer three products. Serve Link helps connect robots in the field to AI systems running in data centers, which would allow companies to potentially tap into more powerful AI models without having to put all that computing power onboard.

“Any robotic application generally needs to connect the robots to some offline intelligence, whether it’s to collect data or do exception handling or whatever,” said Kashani. “It’s the connectivity piece that has to be really high performance. You need to be able to manage really unreliable networks and still reliably connect, and that’s what we solve.”

It’s also launching a data curator tool that helps companies find edge cases in the reams of real-world data a robot collects, which can then be fed back into a training model to improve performance. Its third product is a real-world, foundation-model data catalog built from Serve’s own sidewalk robots that can teach AI models how to understand complex human environments.

Kashani said he’s been thinking about this idea — a playbook he learned from Amazon — for years.

“When the technology is so nascent, you have got to build the end-to-end application because that’s the only way you know what to build, but then over time, as the technology gets more advanced, a lot more people are going to be wanting to build similar things,” he said. “And what you want to do is to open your technology so others build with you and on your platform.”

Wall Street apre in altalena. Il Dow Jones perde lo 0,94% a 51.060,72 punti, il Nasdaq sale dell'1,22% a 24.625,96 punti mentre lo S&P 500 avanza dello 0,39% a 7.383,46 punti.

Restano forti vendite sui mercati azionari europei, che girano la boa di metà seduta sempre in ampio negativo. La Borsa peggiore è quella di Francoforte che cede il 2,2%, seguita da Londra in calo di due punti percentuali. Pesanti Parigi (-1,6%) e Amsterdam (-1,2%), con Madrid e Milano che provano a contenere i ribassi e segnano un calo attorno al punto percentuale.

Oscillano sempre attorno alla parità con una leggera intonazione positiva i future sull'avvio di Wall Street specie, sui titoli hi tech che hanno trainato lo scivolone di ieri. E quindi per l'indice Nasdaq.

Nel settore energia il gas conferma il suo calo e cede il 3% a 88 euro al Megawattora, mentre il petrolio si muove calmo sui 90 dollari dollari al barile. Senza grandi variazioni i titoli di Stato con lo spread Btp-Bund sui 109 euro, con l'euro che conferma il calo dello 0,4% a 1,117 contro il dollaro.

Con gli operatori che cominciano a guardare anche alle prossime scelte della Bce, in Piazza Affari tra i titoli a maggiore capitalizzazione Nexi accusa un calo del 3,8%, Generali di tre punti percentuali e il Banco Bpm del 2,7% dopo i conti resi noti ieri a mercati chiusi. Debole anche Unipol (-2,6%), mentre Mps è limata dello 0,7% dopo la trimestrale. Bene invece Technoprobe e Stm, che recuperano il 2,5% e il 2,6% dopo i pesanti ribassi della vigilia.

Anche i mercati azionari asiatici e dell'area del Pacifico chiudono tutti in calo sulla scia dello scivolone di Wall Street e dei i timori legati ai risultati delle elezioni statunitensi, che tra l'altro potrebbero rallentare gli investimenti nei data center dedicati all'intelligenza artificiale. I listini più pesanti sono Seul che ha ceduto il 6% netto e Tokyo in calo del 5,9%.

Negative anche le Borse cinesi, con Shenzhen che ha perso il 2,2% e Shanghai l'1,1%. In calo del'1,2% Hong Kong, mentre Sidney ha contenuto il ribasso di mezzo punto percentuale. Negativi i future sull'avvio dei listini europei, ancora incerti quelli su Wall street.

La Borsa di Tokyo termina la seduta con l'indice di riferimento sotto quota 60.000 punti per la prima volta in circa cinque mesi e mezzo.

Il listino di riferimento Nikkei segna una flessione del 5,96% a quota 57.434,77, con una perdita di 3.643 punti. Sul mercato valutario lo yen si rafforza sul dollaro a 157,80, e sull'euro a 176,70.

Capire l’economia e la finanza per scegliere il futuro. Young Factor Europe porta l’educazione economico-finanziaria nelle scuole superiori di sei Paesi, con una piattaforma gratuita e un percorso costruito su 50 parole chiave. Andrea Ceccherini, fondatore e presidente di Osservatorio for Independent Thinking, ha presentato la nuova edizione a Milano davanti alla presidente Bce Christine Lagarde e a 600 studenti.

Ceccherini: «Esercizio per partecipare alla vita democratica»

La posta in gioco supera la gestione dei risparmi: «Studiare la finanza e l’economia – spiega Ceccherini – è oggi un esercizio per partecipare a pieno titolo alla democrazia». Quello dell’alfabetizzazione economico-finanziaria,ha commentato la governatrice della Bce, è «un tema che mi sta particolarmente a cuore e che considero una componente essenziale della libertà: in particolare per le donne, conoscere gli strumenti finanziari e disporre delle competenze necessarie per gestire le proprie risorse significa poter compiere scelte autonome e decidere del proprio futuro». Da qui il «ringraziamento» all’Osservatorio per l’alto valore civile dell’iniziativa e «per il lavoro che sta facendo».

Le Cinquanta parole

termini Il progetto è in fase pilota avanzata in Italia, Germania e Spagna e avviata in Francia, Paesi Bassi e Portogallo. Nel nostro Paese il progetto è sostenuto da Intesa Sanpaolo e UniCredit ai quali si aggiungerà anche Crédit Agricole Italia.

Il fulcro sono 50 parole, spiegate e illustrate, che si affrontano in cinque anni: test per misurare le conoscenze, videolezioni, attualità, masterclass dei governatori delle banche centrali e attività pratiche. A disposizione di docenti e studenti il giornalismo di Financial Times, The Economist, Wall Street Journal e Sole 24 Ore, attraverso la piattaforma Doubt and Debate.

Lagarde: «Questioni finanziarie ancora poco capite»

Quanto sia necessario questo alfabeto lo indica la stessa Lagarde parlando davanti agli studenti a Milano: in Europa, osserva, «il 50% dei cittadini ha una comprensione molto limitata delle questioni finanziarie. C’è chi fatica a distinguere un tasso fisso da uno variabile». Lacune che si riflettono sulla capacità di valutare un’offerta, gestire le proprie risorse e decidere con consapevolezza.

articles.body:
LONDON – The Bank of England (BOE) raised interest rates for the first time in over three years on Thursday and warned that at least one more increase was likely if the U.S.-Iran conflict continues, as it started on a path already begun by its main peers.

British inflation is likely to rise to around 5% in the middle of next year, the BOE said, more than double the central bank’s target and a blow to Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has sought to ease cost of living pressures.

The BOE found little evidence so far of faster inflation outside sectors directly hit by higher energy costs. However, policymakers said that the amount of inflation pressure coming down the road after months of high energy prices required a rate rise now, even though that will increase borrowing costs for businesses and many home owners.

articles.title: Commentary: Who keeps crashing China’s stock market?
articles.summary: Over the past decade, the domestic market has endured at least three bear runs that prompted emergency government bailouts, says Shuli Ren for Bloomberg Opinion.
articles.preview: Over the past decade, the domestic market has endured at least three bear runs that prompted emergency government bailouts, says Shuli Ren for Bloomberg Opinion. HONG KONG: China is scrambling to contain a stock market rout only two years after the previous rescue. Beijing is dusting off the market support playbook it deployed in 2024. The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) is providing low-cost funding for corporate share buybacks and liquidity for institutional investors.
articles.body:
Over the past decade, the domestic market has endured at least three bear runs that prompted emergency government bailouts, says Shuli Ren for Bloomberg Opinion.

HONG KONG: China is scrambling to contain a stock market rout only two years after the previous rescue.

Beijing is dusting off the market support playbook it deployed in 2024. The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) is providing low-cost funding for corporate share buybacks and liquidity for institutional investors. The shadowy “national team” appears to have stepped up its operations, while regulators are again resorting to window guidance – informally instructing institutional investors and brokerages not to sell.

In October, China’s stock market suffered its worst monthly decline in more than a decade. The blue-chip CSI 300 Index has fallen into a bear market from its late-June peak, while Shanghai’s semiconductor-heavy SSE Science and Technology Innovation Board 50 Index, or Star 50, has plunged as much as 48 per cent.

THE BLAME GAME

So who’s been selling? The blame game has already begun.

Shiva Capital Group, one of China’s biggest hedge funds, has pointed the finger at insurers. In a recent letter to clients, founder Hong Liang accused the insurance firms of piling into technology stocks near their July peak, only to slash positions in late September. The behaviour was “truly baffling”, lamented the prominent investor, who has a large following on the mainland.

Liang certainly has reason to deflect blame. China has a long history of faulting private sector investors, from quant funds to foreign asset managers, for igniting selloffs. But he might just have a point this time.

China had already endured a bear market in July, when momentum-driven trades suffered their worst loss in history. The pattern mirrored markets in South Korea and the United States, where the red-hot semiconductor trade was hastily unwound.

NOT THE USUAL SUSPECTS

Three months later, however, the usual suspects are harder to blame. Margin financing has already fallen, as has northbound turnover through the Stock Connect with Hong Kong, suggesting neither leveraged traders nor foreign hot money is behind the latest weakness.

That leaves a different potential offender: long-only institutional investors.

State-owned insurers have been steadily increasing their stock holdings in recent years. China Life Insurance, for instance, has scaled up artificial-intelligence-related bets and raised its equity allocation to 19.2 per cent of its portfolio by the end of June, from 16.9 per cent in 2025.

Beyond the hunt for higher returns, insurers have been responding to policymakers, who want them to provide more long-term capital to the stock market – a priority that the head of China’s securities regulator reiterated in a high-profile speech in mid-June. Talk about bad timing.

In recent days, authorities have issued window guidance to several major insurers, requiring them to report their equity holdings, refrain from cutting their losses, and align investment decisions with broader economic goals.

WHO WILL BE LEFT TO BLAME?

The government now appears to be grappling with an unintended consequence of its own policy.

Insurers may be more patient investors than hedge funds, but they still have to manage risk and meet claims and other liabilities. That limits their ability to sit indefinitely on mounting losses – and can force them to cut exposure during severe market downturns.

Insurers, in other words, cannot be as reliably countercyclical as the “national team”, whose primary purpose is market stabilisation.

On its latest earnings call, executives at China Pacific Insurance Group acknowledged that equity investing had become “complicated” and that portfolios needed to be managed so market volatility didn’t damage short-term returns. In the third quarter, profits at China’s five major listed insurers plunged, largely because of the decline in domestic stocks.

The experience points to an uncomfortable reality: For insurers, reliable dividend payers such as Bank of Jiangsu may ultimately be better suited to their liabilities than capital-intensive chipmakers.

Few in China – including Shiva’s Liang – are willing to say publicly that policy missteps themselves may be contributing to poor stock market performance. Instead, blame has fallen on everything from thin liquidity to indiscriminate selling.

But that raises a bigger question: Why does China keep suffering stock market routs? Over the past decade, the domestic market has endured at least three bear runs that prompted emergency government bailouts – in 2018, 2024 and now.

The next time the PBOC has to put out a fire, who will be left to blame? Foreigners, hedge funds and now even state-owned insurers have all had their turn.
